standfirst: For the first time the whole United Nations membership has agreed that a state does not stop being a state when its territory goes under water, and that its ocean boundaries hold where its coastline does not — and the United States did not block it. In the same week NATO published the first revision of its resilience baseline in a decade, with extreme weather written in and the words climate change written out, while a British foreign secretary told the security community that climate belongs in threat assessments and then routed £1 million of a £331 million package to the only standing multilateral machinery the field has. Somalia's government and the United Nations asked for money to act on a flood forecast that is about as close to certain as forecasts get, and did not get it.
orientation:
Claims carry one of three marks. **Evidence** is what the sources actually support. **Contested** is where researchers or practitioners genuinely disagree. **Framing** is advocacy, policy narrative or institutional positioning. **Gap** is a verified absence — something looked for and not found. Sections A and D do not use the marks: A is curriculum reading, D is attributed action.

One operation runs through the whole week, and it runs in both directions at once: the climate referent and the security register are being pulled apart. NATO revised its seven baseline requirements for resilience for the first time since 2016, and the revision names extreme weather, natural disasters and changing environmental conditions while the phrase climate change appears nowhere in it — the hazard kept, the cause unnamed. A United States president addressed the General Assembly and his own government's summary of what he said contains no climate and no energy at all, a year after climate was the centrepiece of the same speech. India's foreign minister organised his statement around a weaponisation of everything and named chokepoints in finance, markets, supply chains and technology, with climate handled separately and in the development register. Running the other way, a British foreign secretary stood up at Climate Week and asked for climate to be put into threat assessments and contingency planning by the generals rather than the campaigners, and a British, European and Kenyan trio convened foreign ministers on climate and ecosystem degradation as national security risks.

Read B1 against D4 for the point. The most consequential thing the field won this week was won in neither register: the sea-level declaration is an instrument about sovereignty, statehood and the law of the sea, and that is very likely why it passed by consensus in a year when climate language could not have. Then read D2 against D1 to see what the field's own vocabulary is currently worth in money: three tenths of one per cent of the package announced under it.
housekeeping:
**Sourcing.** Most of what follows rests on documents opened and read this week: the General Assembly President's page and concept note for the sea-level meeting, the United Nations meetings coverage of that meeting, the World Meteorological Organization's own note on the declaration, Columbia Law School's climate law blog, Grist, Climate Home News, NATO's own official text of the 2026 resilience baseline requirements and its announcement of them, NATO's environment and climate topic page, the Council on Strategic Risks' front page and its analysis of the NATO document, the World Food Programme's and UNICEF's joint release on Somalia, the United Nations in Somalia's page for this year's humanitarian plan, the Food and Agriculture Organization's earlier flood warning, gov.uk for the Foreign Secretary's Climate Week speech and for the co-hosts' statement from the foreign ministers' dialogue, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's funding announcement, the Kathmandu Post's transcript of Nepal's address to the General Assembly and its columns, China's own foreign ministry text of the twenty-fifth round of boundary talks with India, the Planetary Security Initiative's team page, the International Military Council on Climate and Security's own site, SIPRI's climate-security publications list, adelphi's publications index, The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies' news index, the Netherlands Court of Audit's report on North Sea infrastructure, the Dutch parliament's agenda for 24 September, the European Parliament research service's briefing on the coming resilience framework, and the White House's own summary of the presidential address. Section A citations were checked against Crossref. Coordinates come from Wikipedia's coordinates interface.

**What would not open.** Clingendael's own publications pages refused retrieval for a third consecutive week, so everything Dutch and institutional here again rests on the Planetary Security Initiative's separate site and on search rather than on the institute itself. The Alliance of Small Island States' statements and documents pages refused retrieval, so its position this week is taken from the President of Palau's remarks as the United Nations recorded them rather than from the alliance's own text. The Loss and Damage Fund's own site refused retrieval, which matters more than usual: the standing question about who chairs its board and when it next meets still rests on press reporting, and the fund's own financial reporting was not read. The publisher's page for the recent article in section A refused retrieval, so the reading of it rests on the database record and the abstract as reproduced elsewhere; the same is true of the closing item of the curriculum phase, whose full text was not read and whose argument is summarised here from secondary accounts and should be treated accordingly. The trust fund that finances the multilateral climate-security unit lists a 2025 financial report whose figures did not render, so the standing question about that unit's funding trajectory has a route now but still not an answer. The Dutch government's central document register was reorganised earlier this year and its replacement could not be searched from here, which is why the absence recorded in section C for the Netherlands is stated as weaker than a verified absence.

**Corrections to the published record.** Four.

First and largest: last week this digest recorded that NATO's silence on its lapsed annual climate and security assessment had continued for a third consecutive week and that continued silence was itself the finding. NATO had in fact published, three days before that week closed, the first revision of its seven baseline requirements for resilience since 2016, and released them publicly for the first time. The lapsed assessment is still lapsed and the topic page still shows 2022, 2023 and 2024 and nothing since. But scoring the week as silence missed the actual move, which is more interesting than the absence: see D4.

Second, on the same page. Last week's reading of NATO's environment and climate topic page reported the most recent item of any kind on it as dating from June 2025. This week's reading of the same page gives a page last updated in July 2024, with nothing after the 2024 assessment. One of the two readings is wrong and it is not possible to say which from here; what both agree on, and what the argument rests on, is that no assessment has appeared for 2025 or 2026.

Third, a conflation in other people's reporting rather than in this digest, flagged because it will spread. Nepal has two separate things in front of the loss and damage fund: $20 million confirmed in early September under the fund's interim route, for proposals submitted earlier in the year and predating the August disaster, with release still pending a reviewer's comments; and a separate emergency request arising from the disaster, acknowledged and not scheduled. Reporting published on 27 September describes the $20 million as the disaster claim. It is not. The two figures happen to coincide because $20 million is also the ceiling for a single project under that route, which is the arithmetic the pushback above turns on.

Fourth, smaller. Two entries on the standing roster have been carrying an unresolved discrepancy about a Dutch researcher's job title and an unverified claim about a retired Dutch general's institutional affiliation. Both are now settled from the platform's own team page and both had been described here more confidently than the evidence warranted; the correction is in the roster rather than in anything a reader was told.

**Length.** Long, and deliberately: five of the seven developments below are institutional texts whose exact wording is the finding, and paraphrase would have destroyed the point.

pushback.target: This digest's own four-week assumption that the central institutional question in the Nepal file is what the Loss and Damage Fund will do, and on what evidentiary basis — the assumption behind the standing questions about the gap between attribution and finance, about the evidence standard a fund would apply, and about whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable
pushback.text:
The assumption was wrong in a way that three weeks of careful work on the evidentiary question could not expose, because the evidentiary question was never binding.

Nepal's claim on the fund is for $20 million. That is not a modest ask that could be argued upward with better evidence; it is the ceiling, the largest single project the fund's interim route will consider. Against a reconstruction and recovery bill the country's own assessment puts at about $4.7 billion, the instrument's maximum is roughly four tenths of one per cent. And the fund has paid nobody anything. At least 119 countries have asked it for about $2.8 billion in total; a board meeting in June looked at four requests and approved none; the next is not until December. Of about $822 million pledged, something between a third and a half has actually arrived.

So the question this digest has been asking — what standard of proof will a fund board apply to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution — presumes a board that adjudicates. Framed that way it elevated an evidentiary puzzle, which is intellectually interesting and has a literature, over an arithmetic one, which is neither. When an instrument's ceiling is three orders of magnitude below the claim and its disbursement record is zero, the standard of evidence it would apply is not the constraint. It is a detail about a door that is not open.

The correction is not that loss and damage does not matter. It is about where the live institutional question sits, and this week Nepal's own prime minister answered that from the General Assembly rostrum. He did ask for finance, and called the fund and the other mechanisms grossly inadequate, and warned against climate finance becoming a maze in which vulnerable countries spend years proving they need help. But the thing he proposed building was not a financing instrument. It was a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism with India and China in it, to share satellite data, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, run joint early warning and coordinate assistance across borders. That is a demand for an institution rather than a transfer, and it is aimed at exactly the transboundary data wall this digest has tracked since the beginning of September. The financing question is a queue; the data question is a mechanism that does not exist. A tracker that spends its attention on the queue will be watching the wrong thing when the mechanism either forms or fails.

One thing survives intact from the old framing, and it is worth restating because it now has to be carried alongside the correction rather than inside it. An adaptation-limits argument still has no institutional procedure anywhere, and the first body that reaches for one will set the standard by default. That remains true. It is simply not what is holding up the money.

citation.author: Marc A. Levy
citation.title: Is the Environment a National Security Issue?
citation.verification_note: Author's given name confirmed as Marc A. Levy against the Crossref record for the DOI; the reading list carried the surname only and warned that it had not been checked. Crossref gives International Security 20(2), 1995, first page 35, and as with every other item in this phase it records only the opening page, so the closing page rests on the issue record, which independently gives Fall 1995, 35-62. Full text not read: the copies reachable from here refused retrieval, and the summary below rests on the article's abstract record and on secondary accounts of its argument rather than on the article itself.

foundational.summary: Levy closes the phase by sorting environment-and-security claims into three kinds and treating them differently. The existential claim — that some parts of the environment are so bound up with a country's deepest values that harming them is ipso facto a security threat — he attributes to Jessica Tuchman Mathews and Norman Myers and dismisses as having no basis except as a rhetorical device for mobilising support. The physical claim, that a specified environmental change damages a specified national interest, he treats as the serious one, because it can be tested and can fail; and he accepts that ozone depletion and climate change could threaten core American values directly and so qualify. The political claim, that environmental issues matter because they reshape politics, he treats as real but secondary. The effect is to convert the Mathews-Deudney argument from a dispute about principle into a question of magnitude and specificity, and to make the answer country-specific: for the United States in the mid-1990s, he is sceptical that conflicts driven by environmental scarcity elsewhere reach American interests. It is a verdict on the exchange rather than a fourth position in it, which is why the reading list puts it here.
critiques: The most durable criticism is that Levy's own test cuts both ways. Having conceded that climate change can qualify as a direct threat under the physical argument, he then reasons about near-term American exposure and concludes that most regional environmental problems do not reach it — which is a claim about timing, not about the category, and timing is the one thing thirty years have settled against him.

Reviewers at the time objected that the categories are not as separable as the article needs them to be: land, fuelwood and water scarcity in other countries were, on their reading, the more pressing problems precisely because their political effects travel, which collapses his second and third categories into each other.

From the critical strand the objection is the opposite one, and is not answered here: by accepting the physical argument on the security establishment's own terms, Levy grants that establishment the authority to decide what counts, which is the move Deudney's essay was written to refuse. Levy adjudicates the exchange from inside one of its positions.

A limitation of this week's reading rather than of the article: the full text could not be opened, so the account above is reconstructed and any reader relying on it should check the original before quoting the taxonomy.

citation.author: Michael J. Strauss
citation.title: Challenges to peace arising from the reconfiguration of state territory amid the sea level rise
citation.venue: Journal on the Use of Force and International Law
citation.verification_note: Author, title, venue, pagination, publication date and DOI confirmed against the Crossref record, which also gives the author's affiliations as the Centre d'Etudes Diplomatiques et Stratégiques in Paris and the Université Catholique de Lille, and records the article as received and accepted on 8 March 2026. The publisher's page refused retrieval, so the reading below rests on the abstract as reproduced by search indexes rather than on the full text, and the volume and issue are not yet assigned.

foundational.summary: Chosen because this week's central development is a political declaration about what happens to states whose territory goes under water, and this is the most recent peer-reviewed treatment of the same problem from the use-of-force side rather than the law-of-the-sea side. Strauss's premise is that sea-level rise is not a small-island problem but a general one: a majority of states will lose land, at different rates and in different amounts, and the result is a new and involuntary redistribution of territory. His argument is that this redistribution creates territorial inequalities that did not previously exist, and that a state severely enough affected may come to calculate that the human, material and legal costs of taking land from a neighbour are the lesser evil. He then asks whether existing international law, and the law of the sea in particular, is equipped to keep the peace under those conditions. The interest for this field is that it is a structural argument about incentives rather than a threat-multiplier argument about instability, and it puts the conclusion where security institutions can act on it: the pressure is not on fragile states, it is on borders.
critiques: The mechanism is deductive. There is no case, no dataset and no historical instance of territorial loss to the sea producing a use of force, so the paper's central move — that a state may judge conquest the lesser evil — is an argument from incentives and not a finding. The empirical literature on interstate water conflict, which the reading list reaches in phase 5, is the standing warning about exactly this form of reasoning: the predicted wars did not happen.

It sits uneasily beside the week's declaration. If the presumption is that statehood and maritime zones survive physical loss, then the legal incentive Strauss describes weakens considerably, because the thing a state would be fighting for — recognised territory and its attached maritime entitlements — is precisely what the declaration says it does not lose. The paper predates the declaration and cannot be faulted for that, but the two should be read against each other rather than in sequence.
The reading is incomplete for the reason given above: the full text was not available, so the typology of cases and the treatment of the law of the sea are known only from the abstract.

developments.title: The General Assembly declares that statehood and maritime zones survive the loss of territory to the sea
developments.body: At a high-level plenary meeting convened under the eighty-first General Assembly, states adopted by consensus the first United Nations declaration devoted to sea-level rise. Its operative core is legal rather than climatic: it affirms a presumption in favour of continued statehood, so that the disappearance of a state's territory would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood, and it affirms that states which have established maritime zones under the law of the sea can maintain them in the face of physical changes resulting from sea-level rise, without prejudice to their ability to update them. It also commits signatories to enhance anticipatory action, multi-hazard early warning and climate information systems, and to strengthen coordinated scientific observation and data exchange through the global ocean and sea-level observing systems. The process behind it was mandated by a General Assembly decision in 2024 and co-facilitated by the permanent representatives of Australia and Cabo Verde, James Martin Larsen and Tania Serafim Yvonne Romualdo; the negotiated text passed a silence procedure in August. The Secretary-General told the meeting that rising seas are sinking futures, and that sea-level rise is measured in millimetres but its toll in millions of shattered lives. The Netherlands, speaking for a country that has lived below the sea for centuries and whose Caribbean islands face retreating beaches and storm surge now, offered to share its knowledge of water management, coastal protection and freshwater security, and said that the sea is patient and takes a little more each year, and that what it takes it does not easily return.
developments.arc_note: Novel in form, not in argument. Small island states have made the statehood and maritime-zone case for over a decade, the International Law Commission concluded a six-year study of sea-level rise in international law in 2025 finding strong state support for continuity, and the International Court of Justice touched the question in its 2025 advisory opinion. What is new is that the whole membership has now said it in a single negotiated instrument, which converts a scholarly and litigated position into state practice.

attribution.note: No single event is at issue. The observational anchor the meeting used is the World Meteorological Organization's: global mean sea level at the end of 2025 stood about 11 centimetres above its January 1993 level, and the rate has accelerated over the satellite era. The Organization's own note stresses that significant observational gaps remain, particularly across the oceans, in small island developing states and in other vulnerable coastal regions — which is the reason the declaration's observation commitments are not decoration.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The declaration affirms a presumption in favour of continued statehood and the stability of established maritime zones, and was adopted by consensus with no state formally objecting.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The United States did not block the text. That is the single most surprising fact in this digest this week, and it is a fact about the register the instrument was written in rather than about American climate policy, which moved in the opposite direction in the same building two days earlier (B6).

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Bryce Rudyk explains the consensus in one line — everyone will lose land, and no one wants to lose ocean — arguing that every coastal state benefits from a rule that freezes maritime entitlements. It is the most economical available explanation and it should be marked as interested: Rudyk is an adjunct professor at New York University's law school and director of its United Nations diplomacy clinic, and has been legal adviser to the Alliance of Small Island States since 2013. The State Department declined to comment, so the American reasoning is not on the record at all.

source.title: UN passes first declaration on sea level rise, protecting island nations' sovereignty

claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether continuity of statehood follows from existing law is genuinely disputed among lawyers, and the dispute is on the record rather than in the air. The International Law Commission's final report in 2025 found strong support among states for continuity, grounding it in self-determination, territorial integrity and the avoidance of statelessness. Judge Tomka of Slovakia dissented from the International Court of Justice's 2025 treatment of the question, arguing that the 1933 Montevideo Convention's four criteria govern the continuation of a state and not merely its creation — which, if right, means a state without territory or population has no continuing legal personality to preserve.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: A political declaration creates no binding obligation. Its work is done through state practice: a consensus text of the whole membership is the kind of evidence a tribunal weighs when asking what states believe the law to be, which is why the instrument is worth more than its legal form suggests and less than its supporters will say.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing in the reachable record connects this instrument to any security institution. No defence ministry, alliance staff or intelligence body was reported as engaging it, and the declaration itself is not framed in the security register — no threat multiplier, no instability, no displacement argument. An instrument that settles the sovereignty and maritime-entitlement status of dozens of states is a first-order security document and is not currently being read as one.

nl_eu.note: Direct twice over. The Netherlands spoke, and framed itself as a knowledge exporter on water management, coastal protection and freshwater security while naming its own Caribbean islands as exposed now rather than later — which is the first time in this digest's record that a Dutch multilateral intervention has put the Caribbean part of the kingdom in the same sentence as the delta. For the European Union the maritime-zone half matters more than the statehood half: frozen baselines mean frozen fishing and seabed entitlements for member states' own overseas territories, and the Union's external maritime boundaries with third states stop being a function of erosion.

developments.title: Somalia's government and the United Nations ask for money against a flood forecast that is close to certain
developments.body: The federal government, the Food and Agriculture Organization, UNICEF and the World Food Programme issued a joint warning that the latest food-security classification projects 5.4 million people in crisis-level hunger or worse between October and December, of whom 1.5 million reach emergency level, alongside 1.92 million children under five needing treatment for acute malnutrition over the year to June 2027 and 433,000 of them severely acutely malnourished. The same statement carries the disaster agency's estimate that between 2.5 and 3.5 million people are exposed to the flooding expected in the October-to-December rains, with about a million likely to be displaced from the land they farm and graze. The humanitarian coordinator for Somalia, George Conway, described the situation as dire; the disaster agency's commissioner, Mohamuud Moallim Abdullahi, said the concern was sharpened by preparation for the El Niño impacts. What the statement asks for is not assessment but money, in one phrase: urgent funding is needed to turn early warnings into action, and to pre-position supplies before flooding closes the roads in October.
developments.arc_note: The pattern is the Horn of Africa's standard one — a strong El Niño with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole producing enhanced rainfall and riverine flooding on the Juba and Shabelle, as in 2023 and 1997. What is accelerating is the gap between forecast quality and response capacity. The forecast is about as strong as seasonal forecasts get: a hundred per cent probability of El Niño conditions from mid-2026 into early 2027, 23 of 26 models projecting a very strong event peaking in October to December, and dipole probabilities above 80 per cent for September to November. Against that, this year's humanitarian plan asks $852 million to reach 2.4 million people, which is itself a 40 per cent reduction on the 2025 appeal.

attribution.note: No event has happened yet, and nobody is claiming one has been attributed. The causal statement in play is about a climate mode rather than about warming: El Niño with a positive dipole raises Horn of Africa rainfall, which is textbook teleconnection and not an anthropogenic claim. Some secondary reporting this week described the El Niño itself as intensified by rising ocean temperatures; no study supporting that was found and the claim is not carried here.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The projection is 5.4 million people at crisis level or worse from October to December, 1.5 million of them at emergency level, with 2.5 to 3.5 million exposed to flooding and about a million likely to be displaced.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: This year's humanitarian plan seeks $852 million to reach 2.4 million people and was launched in January at 40 per cent below the 2025 requirement. The reduction is in the ask, not in the need; it was set before the seasonal forecast firmed up.

source.title: Humanitarian partners seek US$852 million to assist 2.4 million people in 2026

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Anticipatory action was not a missing idea here. The agriculture organisation's water and land management unit warned in June that the October-to-December season was the flood risk, named the Juba and Shabelle basins, and listed the measures — repair embankments, identify high ground, pre-position supplies, arrange financing before the season. Four months later the same measures are being asked for again, which locates the failure at financing rather than at forecasting or planning.

source.title: FAO warns Somalia to prepare now for potential El Niño-linked flooding later in 2026

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No security institution has engaged this. Nothing was found from the African Union, from the United Nations mission architecture in Somalia, or from any European or American defence body connecting the forecast displacement of a million people in an active conflict theatre to a security assessment. The one place it surfaced in the security register this week was a foreign ministers' statement in New York that named El Niño and promised to mitigate its impact (D1), a day after this warning and with no money attached to that sentence.

source.title: Press statement by co-hosts of the UNGA Foreign Ministers Dialogue on Climate Change and Ecosystem Degradation as National Security Risks

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Read the sequence as an argument about what early warning is for. The field has spent two years treating warning capability as the binding constraint on climate-driven humanitarian loss, and the Himalayan case last week produced a finding that no warning system could have helped. Somalia is the mirror image: the warning is excellent, the lead time is months rather than minutes, the actions are specified, and the loss will happen anyway. Whether warning is the constraint is an empirical question with different answers in different hazard classes, and the field keeps answering it once.

nl_eu.note: Indirect and unflattering. The European Union is among the largest humanitarian donors to the Horn and the Netherlands funds the region bilaterally, so a 40 per cent smaller appeal in a forecast El Niño year is partly a European decision rather than an act of nature. It also bears directly on the migration-and-border framing that dominates European climate-security discourse: a million people displaced inside Somalia in the fourth quarter is the upstream event that European institutions describe downstream and at the Mediterranean.

developments.title: Typhoon Dujuan sets a station rainfall record on Japan's Pacific coast
developments.body: Typhoon Dujuan brought record rainfall, flooding and landslides to eastern Japan on 21 and 22 September. The 48-hour total at Ōshima, in Tokyo's offshore island group, reached 832 millimetres, an all-time record for the station; Miura in Kanagawa recorded 365.5 millimetres and the Yamate station in Yokohama 342. The national fire and disaster management agency reported 12 dead and three missing as of 24 September, seven of the deaths in Chiba, four in Kanagawa and one in Miyazaki. Close to two million people in and around Tokyo were under evacuation advisories at the peak, tens of thousands of households lost power, homes collapsed and hundreds of flights were cancelled.
developments.arc_note: Typhoon flooding in eastern Japan is a repeat pattern in the most literal sense — it is what the country's warning, evacuation and building systems are built for. The acceleration is in the intensity envelope rather than in the frequency: an all-time station record for two-day rainfall is a statement about the ceiling moving, and it is the kind of observation that matters to a high-capacity state because a record broken is a design assumption invalidated.

attribution.note: No attribution study exists as of the close of this week. The rapid-attribution network's own by-year listing shows nothing after its Himalaya study of 17 September. Following the correction this digest made last week, that absence is evidence about how long the work takes and nothing else; the question worth asking is whether a case has been declined, and no refusal was found. Secondary reporting attributed the event's intensity to a super El Niño warming ocean temperatures; that is an unsupported causal claim and is not carried here.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The 48-hour rainfall total at Ōshima was 832 millimetres, an all-time record for that station, and the national toll stood at 12 dead and three missing on 24 September.

source.title: Typhoon Dujuan leaves 12 dead and 3 missing, record rain, floods and landslides hit Japan

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Close to two million people were placed under evacuation advisories in and around Tokyo and the casualty count stayed in double figures. That ratio is the finding: it is what a mature warning and evacuation system buys, and it is the correct benchmark against which to read the same hazard class in a state without one.

source.title: Japan's Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 5, forces mass evacuation

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing was found linking the event to Japan's own security or defence planning — no self-defence force mobilisation statement, no reference in a security document, nothing from the alliance structures. Japan is the third-largest economy in the field's usual accounting of climate-exposed military powers and it is effectively absent from the climate-security literature this digest reaches, which is a gap in the coverage as much as in Japan.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Two records in one month in two mountain-adjacent Asian catchments — a station rainfall record here, a deadliest-on-record extreme flow in Nepal in August — will be read together by advocacy and should not be. One is a well-instrumented event in a state with the best civil-protection record in the world; the other killed at least fourteen hundred people. The hazard is comparable and the outcome is not, which is an argument about capacity and not about climate.

nl_eu.note: No Dutch or European link. It is included because it is the week's best available counterfactual for the question the rest of the digest keeps circling: what a rich, prepared, well-warned state loses to a record-breaking rainfall event. The answer is twelve lives and a design assumption, and that number is the measure of what warning and enforcement are worth.

developments.title: The loss and damage fund's ceiling, not its evidence standard, is the constraint
developments.body: Reporting through the week established the arithmetic of the field's largest live test. Nepal's claim on the fund for responding to loss and damage arising from the August disaster is for $20 million, which is the maximum the fund's interim route will consider for a single project. The country's own damage and needs assessment puts reconstruction and recovery at about NPR 723 billion, roughly $4.7 billion, and the finance minister has put the requirement at $4 to $5 billion. Nepal's climate negotiator Raju Pandit Chhetri said the money would be a peanut if it were invested in reconstruction. Two denominators are in circulation and both are the country's own: about $2.7 billion of assessed physical damage and economic loss, against which the claim is 0.7 per cent, and about $4.7 billion of reconstruction and recovery need, against which it is 0.4 per cent. Nothing in the argument turns on which is used. Across the whole fund the position is that at least 119 countries have submitted requests totalling about $2.8 billion, against roughly $822 million pledged of which between a third and a half has arrived; a board meeting in June reviewed four requests and approved none; nothing has been disbursed to anyone; and the next board meeting is in December.
developments.arc_note: This corrects a framing this digest has carried for four weeks rather than reporting something new. The standing trend about the gap between what attribution will certify and what climate finance is asked to pay for, and the standing question about the evidence standard a fund board would apply, both presumed an adjudicating institution. The institution is not adjudicating. See the pushback.

attribution.note: The item is about an instrument, not an event. It is worth noting that the evidentiary question the field spent September on — whether the August cascade could be attributed, and on what basis — has had no bearing on any disbursement decision, because there have been none to have a bearing on.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Nepal's claim is for $20 million, which is the per-project maximum under the fund's interim route, against reconstruction needs its own assessment puts at about $4.7 billion. The claim is therefore about four tenths of one per cent of the bill, and could not have been larger.

claims.text: At least 119 countries have asked the fund for about $2.8 billion in total; 93 per cent of the requests concern extreme events and over three quarters include slow-onset adaptation needs such as sea walls. claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether the delay is administrative or deliberate is disputed, and one side of it is now in print: Tarun Gopalakrishnan of Tufts University argues that the slowness of both the disbursals and the setting up of the fund has been deliberate, a practical evasion of responsibility, and that wealthy states resist money labelled loss and damage because of what the label implies about liability. The fund's own account, which could not be read because its site refused retrieval, is presumably that a new institution is building fiduciary systems. Both explanations fit the observed facts, which is why this is marked contested rather than evidence.

At the General Assembly its prime minister called the fund, the Global Environment Facility and the other relevant mechanisms grossly inadequate, and warned against climate finance becoming a bureaucratic maze in which vulnerable countries spend years proving they need help. A claimant that describes the instrument it is claiming from in those terms is building a case for a different instrument.

developments.title: The China-India river mechanism meeting that both governments announced for September did not happen
developments.body: On 25 August, at the twenty-fifth round of talks between the Chinese and Indian special representatives on the boundary question, the two governments agreed eight points. The seventh reads, in China's own foreign ministry's English text, that the two sides agreed to hold the next meeting of the China-India Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers in September and maintain communication on issues including hydrological data sharing, and renewal of relevant memoranda of understanding. September has now ended with no announcement from either government that the meeting took place. The mechanism dates from 2006 and is the only standing institutional channel for flood-season hydrological data on the Yarlung Tsangpo and Brahmaputra; India had used the preceding boundary-affairs meeting on 6 August to ask for that data and for technical details of the hydropower cascade China is building on the river. Separately, China has continued to supply Nepal's hydrology and meteorology department with daily data from the basin affected by the August disaster, under no agreement; the Nepali hydrologist Binod Parajuli has said that Chinese participants at talks in May explained they did not have the authority to sign a data-sharing agreement and proposed continuing the discussion.
developments.arc_note: The pattern this digest has called the high-mountain warning mismatch, in its institutional half: transboundary hazard, no data-sharing mechanism, and repeated statements of intent that do not convert. What the Parajuli detail adds is a mechanism for the non-conversion that is not simply Chinese refusal — a delegation without signing authority is a different problem from a state that has decided against, and it points at where in the Chinese system the decision actually sits.

attribution.note: An institutional non-event. Nothing to attribute.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: China's own foreign ministry text of the 25 August outcomes commits both sides to holding the expert-level mechanism meeting in September and to communication on hydrological data sharing and the renewal of memoranda of understanding.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No record of the meeting having been held was found from either government or from Indian or Chinese media through 27 September. This is a verified absence against a dated, jointly published commitment, which is the strongest form this digest's China and India gaps have taken: previous weeks recorded the absence of a doctrinal text nobody had promised. Here the promise is in writing and the month is over.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: China is sharing data with Nepal daily without an instrument, and has said it will work towards an agreement and a regular cooperation mechanism. Voluntary daily transfers and a signed obligation are different goods: the first can be withdrawn, and the record of Brahmaputra and Sutlej data sharing being suspended in 2022 is the reason downstream states want the second.

claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether Chinese data practice amounts to strategic withholding is argued rather than established. Ashok Kantha, writing as a former Indian ambassador to China, argues China has an entrenched habit of treating river data as a strategic asset, and cites the 2022 suspensions and the unrenewed monsoon-season agreements. The counter-instance is in the same file: China shares year-round with five Mekong states and is currently sharing daily with Nepal. An interested former envoy's characterisation and a demonstrable pattern of selective sharing are both real and are not the same claim.

If the field wants to argue that climate risk requires institutions rather than goodwill, this is the case that tests the claim, and the European Union has no part in it.

developments.title: Climate disappears from the American presidential address it led a year ago
developments.body: President Trump addressed the General Assembly's general debate on 22 September. The White House's own summary of the speech, published the same day under the title While Others Have Talked, I Have Acted, contains no reference to climate change, global warming, energy policy, renewables or the Paris Agreement; its topics are Iran, terrorism, Western hemisphere security, opposition to global governance and global taxes, artificial intelligence regulation, immigration enforcement and sovereignty. Climate appears in the speech itself in one place, as an analogy used to dismiss a different regulatory demand: the same people, he said, who claimed we would all be dead in twelve years because of global warming are now saying artificial intelligence will kill us all. In the equivalent address twelve months earlier climate had been a set piece — renewables called a joke, the United Nations' predictions called the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world — and generated its own fact-checks.
developments.arc_note: An acceleration of the trend this digest has called the removal of climate from American security vehicles, and a new stage of it. The earlier stages were removal from documents, from budget lines and from vocabulary while the argument against climate policy was still being made loudly. This is the stage after that: the argument is no longer worth making. De-prioritisation is complete when a subject is not even attacked.

attribution.note: A speech. Included as an observable of political salience, not as an event.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The White House's own summary of the 22 September address contains nothing on climate, energy, renewables or the Paris Agreement. For an administration that has made climate policy a signature target, the absence from its own readout is a stronger signal than anything it said.

claims.label: evidence

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The contrast with 2025 is documented rather than remembered: that year's address drew dedicated climate fact-checks over claims that renewables do not work and are too expensive, that the United Nations' climate predictions had not come to fruition, and that emissions reduction costs jobs.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No American defence or intelligence climate output of any kind was found in this window — no installation resilience guidance, no threat assessment language, nothing from the department or the intelligence community. The standing arrangement from the March 2025 secretarial memorandum holds unchanged: references to climate change and related subjects are to be removed from mission statements and planning documents, while hardening installations against extreme weather and assessing weather-related impacts on operations continue. That is the same operation NATO performed this month in its own text (D4), eighteen months later and in a different alphabet.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Set against B1 this produces the week's sharpest puzzle. The administration that will not say the word did not block a consensus United Nations declaration about sea-level rise. The most plausible reading is that the declaration was not, in American eyes, a climate instrument at all: it is about sovereignty, statehood and maritime entitlement, and the United States has coastlines and entitlements of its own to freeze. That is worth knowing as a matter of tactics, and it is not a recommendation: a field that learns to win by not naming its subject will not be able to explain later what it won.

nl_eu.note: Indirect but load-bearing for European planning. European climate-security policy has spent two years arguing with an American position; the position is being vacated rather than defended, which is a different problem. Arguments are answerable and absences are not, and transatlantic working groups constructed to engage a counterpart argument have nothing to engage.

developments.title: Overshoot becomes a planning premise in two instruments, neither of them a security instrument
developments.body: The Secretary-General convened a climate summit at United Nations headquarters on 23 September, alongside a high-level event on climate action and the just transition. Its stated priorities were keeping 1.5°C within reach, mobilising finance for developing countries, and advancing adaptation in an era of climate overshoot; one of its solutions dialogues was titled Financing Adaptation in the Era of Overshoot. Almost a hundred countries announced or restated new emissions targets ahead of the November conference of the parties, though only about half of those have formally submitted them. In the same month the European Parliament's research service published a briefing on the integrated framework for climate resilience the Commission is now due to present on 20 October: a package of a communication, a regulation, a recommendation and a Commission decision whose legislative core includes a common European climate reference scenario for adaptation planning based on a 3°C global warming trajectory by 2100 — described elsewhere as consistent with 2.8 to 3.3°C, the higher figure reflecting that Europe warms faster than the global mean — together with a requirement that member states produce climate resilience strategic plans as a condition of access to European funding, and a duty to assign named risk owners for every major climate risk in key sectors.
developments.arc_note: A decisive acceleration of the trend this digest has tracked since early September as overshoot moving from a risk to a planning premise, and a tightening of what the trend's own tell should be. Two instruments in one month now take exceedance as the planning baseline rather than as a contingency: a Secretary-General's summit names it in a session title, and a European legislative proposal writes a number into the scenario that adaptation plans and funding eligibility will be assessed against. The tell that has still not fired is the one that matters for this field: no security institution uses the term.

attribution.note: Institutional texts and a summit. Nothing to attribute.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The Secretary-General's summit of 23 September set advancing adaptation in an era of climate overshoot as one of three priorities and ran a dialogue titled Financing Adaptation in the Era of Overshoot. This is the first time in this digest's record that overshoot appears in the title of a session at a summit convened by the head of the United Nations.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The coming European framework's legislative core includes a common reference scenario based on a 3°C trajectory by 2100, resilience plans as a precondition of European funding, and mandatory named risk owners for major climate risks; the Commission is scheduled to present it on 20 October and the Environment Council to debate it provisionally on 11 December. The briefing also carries the sentence that climate risks are increasingly recognised as conflict drivers with implications for national security and foreign policy, and puts European adaptation investment needs at about €69 billion a year by 2050.

source.title: European integrated framework for climate resilience (briefing 791469)

claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether a 3°C reference scenario is precautionary or complacent is already disputed. The case for it is that adaptation planning against 1.5°C is planning against a number that will be passed. The case against, argued publicly by climate-risk analysts since the scenario leaked into circulation, is that a central-estimate trajectory understates a 3°C world's tail — tipping elements, compound events and the possibility of higher outcomes — and that a reference scenario used to gate funding becomes a ceiling on what member states plan for rather than a floor.

source.title: How the EU adaptation framework vastly underplays the risk of a 3°C world

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No security institution used the term overshoot in this window. Not NATO, whose own new text this month avoids even the phrase climate change (D4); not a defence ministry; not an intelligence body. The asymmetry is now stark enough to be the finding: the civilian planning system has adopted a trajectory-level premise and written a number into draft law, while the institutions that plan for the consequences of that trajectory have not adopted the vocabulary that describes it.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Guard against the false positive this digest set itself up for two weeks ago. Beyond adaptation limits, which entered circulation on 17 September, is a claim about one event; overshoot as a planning premise is a claim about a trajectory. The European reference scenario is the second kind and counts. An attribution finding about a rock-ice avalanche is the first kind and does not.

nl_eu.note: As direct as it gets. If the framework is adopted as the briefing describes it, every member state including the Netherlands will have to produce a climate resilience strategic plan to access European funding, assessed against a 3°C reference scenario and with named risk owners for major risks. For a country whose statutory delta apparatus already does exactly this, the interesting question is not compliance but arbitrage: the Dutch programme's own scenarios and the European reference scenario will not match, and whichever is used to gate funding becomes the operative one.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The programme under discussion is a documented case of a security priority that is stated and not funded. The Court of Audit reported in May that protection of Dutch North Sea infrastructure is getting off the ground with difficulty: €41.4 million was allocated across 2024 and 2025, the responsible minister asked for €70 million a year from 2026 and received €12.1 million as bridge funding, and an information hub adopted by cabinet to build an integrated picture of the North Sea has stalled because the ministries involved cannot agree who pays and who is accountable. The audit's conclusion is that a current and integrated security picture of the North Sea is still lacking.

claims.text: Independent Dutch strategic analysis went to the same place in the same week. The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies published an episode of its strategy series on 21 September asking whether critical infrastructure at sea can be protected without damaging nature, a week after an episode on how to use the North Sea strategically. The centre's climate, water and food security programme had appeared before that at the Bled Strategic Forum on water security and strategic stability, on 15 September. The domestic security demand that pays for Dutch analysis is currently demand about the North Sea.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No cabinet response to the 2027 delta programme could be found in the twelve days after it was laid before parliament on 15 September. In 2025 the equivalent response arrived one day after the programme. This is recorded as weaker than a verified absence: the Dutch government's central document register was reorganised earlier this year and its replacement could not be searched from here, so the response may exist somewhere this could not reach. If it does not, the standing question about whether the deltacommissaris's ask converts into commitment has now passed two checkpoints without an answer.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No Dutch private-sector climate-security signal was found this week. The one place the private sector enters the Dutch file is as the owner of the offshore assets the state is trying to protect and cannot yet see — wind farms, cables and pipelines, whose operators hold data the state's own audit says is not being shared into a common picture. That is the Dutch instance of the standing problem about publicly indispensable, privately owned infrastructure, and it is a gap in the evidence rather than in the phenomenon.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing new on the defence side. The action plan promised by the July defence climate strategy has still not appeared, now nearly three months on, and the parliamentary defence committee's business this week was a meeting with the European commissioner for defence and space. The €5 million structural line survives in the 2027 budget and remains the whole of Dutch climate-security money as distinct from greening money.

salience.method_note: The recess artefact has passed and this was a normal working week, the second after the budget was laid, so committee agendas are a fair indicator rather than a calendar artefact. Two cautions the other way. First, the week after the general political debate is dominated by departmental estimates and the queue is set months in advance, so the absence of an adaptation debate is weaker evidence than the presence of the North Sea one. Second, and per the standing instruction, none of the operational water-authority activity that occurred this week is counted here: crisis management is not priority-setting.

salience.direction_note: Rising, and for the first time in this digest's record the rise is in the field's own register rather than in an economic-security substitute. The Union's foreign and security policy chief co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, and the Commission's resilience package now has a date and a legislative core.

claims.text: Kaja Kallas, High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the Commission, co-hosted the 24 September foreign ministers' dialogue with the British Foreign Secretary and Kenya's foreign minister, and signed a joint statement committing the co-hosts to analysis and horizon scanning inside national and regional security systems and to joint risk assessments, scenario and contingency planning. This is the Union's external-action side, not its climate side, using the field's own vocabulary.

claims.text: Nothing from the Commission's defence side, from a member-state defence ministry, or from the Union's military structures. The defence commissioner's parliamentary appearance in The Hague this week was on defence and space. The pattern the field should watch is that the Union's climate-security activity runs through diplomacy and civil protection and not through defence, which is the opposite of the American and alliance pattern where defence is the only surviving channel.

The one visible thread is the coming framework's admission that public money cannot cover the cost, which implies a private instrument nobody has specified, and the insurance industry's continuing engagement with the framework, which could not be dated inside this window.

Jaishankar, delivered India's national statement on 26 September, organised around a weaponisation of everything and naming chokepoints in finance, market access, supply chains and technology. claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The joint United Nations climate security unit received £1 million from the United Kingdom on 25 September, inside a £331 million package. That is the first datable figure for the unit's income in five weeks of asking, and it confirms the unit is in an extended third phase to 2028 with ten advisers deployed, the most recent to the Pacific Islands Forum in June. It is also three tenths of one per cent of a package announced under the heading of climate-driven instability.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The climate convention's executive secretary, Simon Stiell, again reached for a register that is not this field's: at Climate Week he framed electrification as shielding countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and called it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy. Security appears fourth and as energy-supply security. The standing question about him — which register he reaches for, not how much security language he uses — produced the same answer as in September's earlier appearance.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing from the Security Council, and nothing from the United Nations peace and security departments in this window. Switzerland takes the Council presidency for October with climate security among its stated thematic priorities, which makes the October programme of work the first datable test of whether the Council's retreat from the term is reversible.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: The multilateral private-sector signal is a verified near-absence rather than an oversight. The ministers' statement commits its co-hosts to examining whether the development banks' crisis-response toolkits are fit for purpose and whether the Fund and the Bank consider climate vulnerability, which is the closest thing to a private-capital commitment anywhere in the week's output, and it is a commitment to examine.

claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether this week represents the field arriving or the field being routed around is genuinely arguable. The optimistic reading is four instruments in seven days. The sceptical reading, which this digest leans towards, is that the two strongest outputs succeeded by not being security instruments at all — a sovereignty declaration and a plurilateral without a secretariat — while the one security institution that legislated this month removed the word from its text. Both readings fit; the discriminating evidence will be whether the joint risk assessments promised on 24 September ever produce a document.

salience.method_note: High-level week inflates every multilateral indicator by construction: it is the one week of the year when heads of government are in the same building and announcements are cheap. A rising judgement taken from this week should be discounted accordingly and re-tested in the second half of October, when the same institutions have to act without an audience.

moves.title: Britain, the European Union and Kenya convene foreign ministers on climate as a national security risk
moves.actor: Ed Miliband, UK Foreign Secretary; Kaja Kallas, High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the European Commission; Musalia Mudavadi, Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs of Kenya
moves.place: New York, on the margins of the eighty-first General Assembly
moves.body: The three co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, and issued a joint press statement. Its commitments are specific enough to be checked later: to regard the climate and nature crisis as a national and global security threat; to conduct analysis and horizon scanning on climate and nature-related risks inside national and regional security systems; to share analysis and undertake joint risk assessments, scenario and contingency planning on the security implications; and to work on transboundary risks, naming fertilisers, food and water security, the expansion of early warning systems and anticipatory action, the adequacy of the multilateral development banks' crisis response toolkits, the treatment of climate vulnerability by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and the embedding of climate security in United Nations agencies. The statement says El Niño is expected to exacerbate existing vulnerabilities and commits the co-hosts to mitigating its impact. Its named forward milestones are the November conference of the parties, the Bank and Fund annual meetings, and continuing engagement through 2027.
moves.stated_rationale: That climate and nature loss are security problems requiring foreign and security ministries rather than environment ministries, and that the risks are transboundary and therefore need shared analysis and joint assessment rather than parallel national work.
moves.inference: Three things are being done here at once, and only one of them is about climate. The first is a venue-construction move: a plurilateral of foreign ministers is the format you choose when the Security Council will not take the file and the climate convention cannot carry a security discussion. The second is a composition move. A European, an African and a British co-host, with the European represented by the Union's security and foreign policy chief rather than its climate commissioner, is a deliberate answer to the standing objection from the Group of 77 that climate security is a Northern securitisation project; Kenya's presence is the load-bearing part of the design. The third is substitution in reverse: for two years this digest has recorded European climate arguments migrating into economic-security and energy-security language because the field's own register was unavailable. Here the Union's own external-action side used the field's register directly, which is the clearest evidence yet that the migration was tactical rather than structural. What the statement conspicuously lacks is a secretariat, a next meeting date, a named deliverable, and money. The commitment to joint risk assessments is the one to watch, because unlike the rest of it that produces a document.

moves.title: Britain puts £331 million behind climate-driven instability and £1 million of it into the field's only standing machinery
moves.actor: Ed Miliband, UK Foreign Secretary, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
moves.body: The day after co-hosting the ministers' dialogue, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office announced £331 million to tackle climate-driven instability and protect vulnerable communities. The breakdown is £330 million to the Global Environment Facility and £1 million to the United Nations Climate Security Mechanism. The stated rationale is that climate shocks beginning in one country travel through supply chains, financial markets and migration patterns to others and reach British consumers directly. Four days earlier the same minister had given the opening keynote at New York Climate Week under the title What climate security means now, arguing that climate breakdown must be an issue for foreign ministers and prime ministers as well as climate ministers, that it belongs to the security community and not just the activist community, to the generals and not just the green campaigners, and that climate and nature must be embedded in national security systems, in threat assessments and in contingency planning. That speech also announced an intended £400 million for a tropical forest facility and restated British carbon budgets aligned to 1.5°C implying an 87 per cent emissions reduction by 2040.
moves.stated_rationale: That climate-driven instability is a direct national security risk to the United Kingdom through supply chains, financial markets and migration, and that supporting vulnerable communities' access to food and water and protecting ecosystems prevents climate-related conflict.
moves.inference: Take the arithmetic seriously, because it is the only hard number the field's own register produced this week. A package announced under the heading of climate-driven instability puts 99.7 per cent of its money into a general environmental fund and three tenths of one per cent into the joint programme that actually deploys climate, peace and security advisers. And the £1 million is a top-up rather than an entry: that programme is already supported by fourteen governments including the United Kingdom, and it is in an extended third phase running to 2028 with ten advisers deployed, the most recent onboarded to the Pacific Islands Forum in June. So this is not new institutional commitment; it is a marginal contribution to an existing pooled fund, announced inside a package whose headline does work the money does not. That said, it is the first datable figure for that unit's income this digest has recorded in five weeks of asking, and a £1 million line item is still a line item: the standing question about whether the mechanism is being wound down can now be answered in the negative for at least one donor. The rhetoric is real, the vocabulary is the field's own, the analysis is competent, and the resource commitment is a rounding error. All four are true at once and the field will want to report only the first three.

moves.title: Nepal proposes a trilateral Himalayan resilience mechanism with India and China
moves.actor: Balendra Shah, Prime Minister of Nepal
moves.body: In Nepal's national statement to the eighty-first General Assembly, the prime minister proposed establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China, to share satellite data and expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, strengthen joint early-warning systems and coordinate assistance across borders when disaster strikes. He set it in the context of the August cascade, citing at least 1,400 confirmed deaths, over 6,000 people still missing and physical recovery needs at about 10 per cent of national output, and argued that climate justice cannot remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations document, that those who contributed more to the problem and have greater capacity to respond must do more, and that the loss and damage fund, the Global Environment Facility and other mechanisms remain grossly inadequate. The rhetorical centre of the speech was a comparison: a world that can deliver a weapon anywhere in seventy-two hours has no excuse for leaving a farmer without the means of a decent livelihood, and intercontinental missiles arrive on time while a peasant in Nepal cannot get fertiliser or fuel at market price.
moves.stated_rationale: That the hazard is transboundary, that monitoring and warning therefore have to be, and that the three states sharing the catchment should share the data and coordinate the response.
moves.inference: This is a claimant switching instruments in public, and it should be read as such. Nepal spent four weeks pressing a financing claim and has now put its most prominent multilateral ask into an institution instead. The design is shrewd on two counts. It asks China for the one thing China has been conspicuously willing to supply informally — daily basin data — and proposes to formalise it inside a body Nepal leads, which is a more attractive frame for Beijing than a bilateral agreement with a downstream state. And it puts India and China in the same mechanism in the month they failed to hold their own scheduled river-data meeting (B5), which makes non-participation costly for both. The obvious weakness is that it was announced from a rostrum rather than agreed in a room: no funding, no secretariat, no responding statement from either of the two states it names, and no date. The other weakness is domestic and was made this week by a Nepali columnist, Sajal Mani Dhital, who argued that attributing the disaster to climate change alone sidesteps institutional responsibility for approving infrastructure in hazardous zones, and that a catchy line at an international forum cannot substitute for accountability at home. A mechanism for sharing warnings does not fix a permitting system that builds in the path of the hazard.

moves.title: NATO rewrites its resilience baseline, keeps the weather and drops the word
moves.actor: NATO; announced by Secretary General Mark Rutte
moves.body: NATO issued the 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements on 15 September and announced them on 17 September, releasing the seven baseline requirements publicly for the first time. It is the first substantial revision since the requirements were set at the Warsaw summit in 2016. Extreme weather, natural disasters, space weather and changing environmental conditions, which inflict increasing strain on resilience across the Euro-Atlantic area, appear among the additional cross-cutting risks. The phrase climate change does not appear in the document. The fourth requirement now obliges allies to maintain comprehensive contingency plans, exercised nationally or with other allies, to secure food and water supply particularly during crisis and conflict, widening a requirement that previously concerned contamination to cover all threats and hazards, and adding objectives on situational awareness, supply continuity and workforce and supply-chain dependencies. The energy requirement now demands mitigation plans for the full spectrum of risks and threats including cascading impacts, with an emphasis on private-sector partnership in resilience investment. The alliance's own announcement quotes the Secretary General on resisting, responding to and recovering from shocks and disruptions, mentions neither climate nor extreme weather, and situates the requirements against hybrid attacks and the commitment allies made to spend up to 1.5 per cent of national output on defence and security including civil preparedness. The American institute that watches this most closely published on it within four days: Erin Sikorsky and Noah Fritzhand at the Center for Climate and Security on 21 September.
moves.stated_rationale: Broadening the requirements to reflect cross-cutting security risks, improving civil-military cooperation, and building resilience through a whole-of-society approach; publishing them to widen the alliance's resilience community beyond governments.
moves.inference:
This is the most important thing NATO has done on this file in two years and it is legible only if you read the document against the announcement. In the text, the hazard is in: extreme weather, natural disasters, changing environmental conditions, an expanded food and water requirement covering all hazards, an energy requirement covering cascading impacts. In the announcement, none of that is mentioned at all, and the framing is hybrid attack and burden-sharing. The cause is nowhere. That is precisely the operation the American defence department performed in March 2025, when a secretarial memorandum ordered references to climate change removed from planning documents while expressly preserving the hardening of installations against extreme weather (B6). NATO has now done the same thing in its own foundational resilience text, and it has done it quietly, in a document that also happens to be the first one it has ever made public.

Two readings are available and they have opposite implications for the field. On the first, this is a substantive defeat dressed as continuity: an alliance that ran an annual climate and security impact assessment from 2022 to 2024 and has now missed two cycles has relocated the surviving work into a hazards framework where climate cannot be named, which means it cannot be argued about, prioritised or funded as climate. On the second, this is how a risk survives a hostile political season: the requirement is binding on allies where an annual assessment never was, and a food and water contingency obligation exercised nationally is worth more in practice than a report. This digest's judgement is that the second reading is correct about the mechanism and the first is correct about the consequence. A requirement that cannot name what is driving the trend it responds to cannot be revised as the trend changes, because there is no variable in the document to revise against. The measurement that would settle it is whether the next revision comes sooner than ten years.

moves.title: Australia opens Climate Week on climate security as national security, and is asked where the plan is
moves.actor: Anthony Albanese, Prime Minister of Australia
moves.body: Australia's prime minister gave the opening keynote at Climate Week in New York, billed by the organisers as climate security is national security. He argued that the energy transition is now a national security priority, described sovereign manufacturing, critical minerals processing and targeted climate finance as reshaping Australia's economic and security framework, warned that the next large-scale disaster is a question of when rather than if, and said that nations cannot afford to forget their Pacific allies in a region where those who have contributed least to the crisis are among the most vulnerable to it. The response from the Australian security community was immediate and hostile. Chris Barrie, a former Chief of the Australian Defence Force speaking for the Australian Security Leaders Climate Group, said that if the prime minister is going to New York to say climate security is national security, Australians are entitled to ask a very simple question: where is the plan — and pointed at continuing coal and gas expansion.
moves.stated_rationale: That the energy transition, critical minerals processing and sovereign manufacturing are national security matters for Australia, and that Pacific vulnerability is an Australian strategic interest.
moves.inference: Australia co-hosts the November conference of the parties with Türkiye and co-facilitated the sea-level declaration adopted three days later (B1), so the positioning is not free-floating: this is a COP co-host establishing the frame it wants the conference read in, and choosing the security frame over the ambition frame. What makes it worth a move rather than a speech is the shape of the objection. Barrie is the same actor type this digest has tracked in three countries — a retired flag officer lending institutional credibility to a climate argument — and he is using that credibility against his own government rather than for it. That is the inverse of the 2007 pattern in which retired officers manufactured an agenda; here the officers are the auditors of an agenda politicians have already adopted. It is a sign of a matured frame, and it is also the frame's most dangerous moment, because the audit is easy to fail: a government that says climate security is national security has volunteered a standard against which its fossil-fuel decisions can be scored, and Australia's exports make that standard expensive.
