roster_silences:
**Silence that is evidence, because the institution has a schedule.** The international military council on climate and security is into an eleventh month: no World Climate and Security Report since 2024 and nothing of any kind on its site since an open letter of 23 October 2025, while its own pages name a chair and a secretary general. An annual report series with named officers and no output is a body kept in existence rather than run. The alliance assessment series it feeds off is in the same condition, listed for 2022, 2023 and 2024 and nothing since — though this week showed where the work went instead, which is the digest's largest correction (D4). The German climate and security conference, the single most useful dated European event in this field, still has no announced 2026 edition; a date that circulated earlier this month could not be confirmed against anything and should not be restated. That is now four consecutive weeks of looking for it, which for an annual fixture is informative.

**Silence that is evidence about how long work takes, and nothing else.** The rapid attribution network has published nothing since 17 September, including nothing on this week's record-breaking Japanese rainfall. Under the rule this digest corrected last week that is not a finding: the question to ask of a research network is whether it has declined a case it was asked to take, and no refusal was found. The Stockholm institute's climate-security list ends in August and shows nothing for September, which is the same kind of silence and should be read the same way. The Berlin institute published one item, an account of its own convening on American energy dynamics on 22 September.

**Silence that cannot be assessed at all.** The Dutch flagship institute's own pages refused retrieval for a third consecutive week, so whether it published this week is unknown rather than negative. This is worth separating from the two categories above every time it happens: an unreachable institution is a hole in the method, not a finding about the institution, and three weeks of it means the Dutch institutional lane in this digest currently rests on a sister platform's pages and on search. What those pages did settle is a personnel question that has been carried unresolved for three weeks and an affiliation this digest twice declined to state; both are now on the record and both had been described here with more confidence than the evidence warranted.

**Not checked this week, and recorded so the gap is visible.** No assessment was made of the African Union, the Gulf states, or the Turkish half of the November conference presidency, which is the outstanding hole on the standing roster with six weeks to go.

watch.title: The October Security Council programme of work
watch.note: Switzerland takes the presidency for October and lists climate security among its stated thematic priorities. The programme of work is published at the start of the month and either contains a climate-related item or does not, which makes this the cleanest datable test in months of whether the Council's move from climate security to natural resource governance is reversible. Watch also whether any item connects to the sea-level declaration adopted this week, which would be the first sign that a security body has read it.

watch.title: Whether India or China answers Nepal's proposal
watch.note: Nepal has proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by itself, India and China, and neither named state had responded by the close of the week. A refusal is as informative as an acceptance. The adjacent datable item is the China-India expert-level meeting on trans-border rivers that both governments publicly scheduled for September and did not hold: if it is quietly held in early October, that is one answer; if it slips again, the mechanism proposal is the only live institutional route left.

watch.title: Whether money moves to Somalia before the rains
watch.note: The Deyr season runs October to December, the forecast is a hundred per cent probability of El Niño with 23 of 26 models projecting a very strong event, between 2.5 and 3.5 million people are estimated exposed to flooding and about a million likely to be displaced, and the appeal was set 40 per cent below last year's. Every condition for anticipatory action except financing is satisfied. Watch for an allocation from the central emergency fund, a donor announcement, or the flooding arriving first. This has a deadline rather than an indicator, which is rare and makes it the most decidable item here.

watch.title: The European resilience framework, 20 October
watch.note: The Commission is scheduled to present the integrated framework for climate resilience on 20 October: a communication, a regulation, a recommendation and a Commission decision, with a common European climate reference scenario based on a 3°C trajectory by 2100, resilience strategic plans as a condition of access to Union funding, and named risk owners for major climate risks. Two things to read for. Whether the 3°C scenario survives into the published text, since a number that gates funding is the most contested thing in the package. And whether the security language in the Parliament's own briefing — that climate risks are increasingly recognised as conflict drivers with implications for national security and foreign policy — appears anywhere in the Commission's, or is confined to civil protection.

active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language, and it is no longer only American. NATO's revised resilience baseline keeps extreme weather, natural disasters and changing environmental conditions and never says climate change, and its announcement says neither; the American defence department adopted the identical formula by memorandum in March 2025. Extended a second way this week: the American presidential address to the General Assembly contains no climate at all in its own government's summary, a year after climate was its set piece. The trend's end state is now visible — the hazard survives, the referent goes, and the subject stops being worth attacking.

US adaptation surviving only where reframed as disaster operations. Partially reversed this week at the level of the institute rather than the state: the climate-security institute's only climate output in the window was an international doctrinal analysis and no new state briefer appeared, which means the statehouse turn is not yet a one-way relocation.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance. Nothing from the Council this week. The October presidency passes to Switzerland, which lists climate security among its stated thematic priorities, so the October programme of work is the first datable test of whether the retreat from the term is reversible.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments. Complicated this week in a way worth holding onto: the membership adopted a consensus declaration with real legal content — a presumption of continued statehood and the stability of maritime zones — and it is not binding and did not need to be, because its work is done as evidence of state practice. The lesson is not that the retreat has reversed but that the field may have been measuring bindingness when it should have been measuring register: an instrument written in sovereignty language passed by consensus in a year when a climate instrument could not have.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment. Confirmed again this week in a second file, which suggests the pattern is about the Dutch state rather than about climate. On the North Sea infrastructure programme the responsible minister asked for €70 million a year from 2026, received €12.1 million as bridge funding after €41.4 million across two years, and the Court of Audit found in May that an information hub adopted by cabinet has stalled because the ministries cannot agree who pays and who is accountable. Programme created, coordination unfunded.

Dutch public-opinion decline against the international average. Not refreshed this week; the evidence is now four months old and unchanged since the May survey. Recorded so the age of the evidence stays visible.

Overshoot moving from a risk to a planning premise. Decisively advanced and now split cleanly in two. In the civilian planning system it has arrived: a Secretary-General's summit dialogue titled Financing Adaptation in the Era of Overshoot, and a coming European regulation whose common reference scenario for adaptation planning is a 3°C trajectory by 2100 with funding eligibility attached to it. In the security system it has not arrived at all, and the institution that legislated this month would not even write climate change. Keep the guard against the false positive: beyond adaptation limits is a claim about one event and is not this.

High-mountain hazard migrating from the mode monitoring was built for to the mode it was not, across borders with no data-sharing mechanism. The border half moved twice this week and in opposite directions. Nepal proposed a trilateral mechanism with India and China from the General Assembly rostrum; and the China-India expert-level meeting that both governments had publicly scheduled for September did not happen. A proposal and a broken appointment, in the same month.

The gap between what event attribution will certify and what climate finance is asked to pay for. Judged this week to have been the wrong frame and kept only as a record of the error: the binding constraint on the claim is arithmetic, not evidentiary. The instrument's per-project ceiling is $20 million against a $4.7 billion bill, and it has paid nobody anything. See the pushback.

Climate argued in whichever security register is locally unoccupied rather than in the field's own. This week the trend needs restating, because it now runs in three directions rather than two. Substitution outward, as before: the climate convention's secretary calling electrification a security strategy, fourth in a list. Substitution inward, which is new: the Union's own foreign and security policy chief using the field's register directly at a foreign ministers' dialogue, which suggests the earlier migration was tactical. And a third case that is neither — the week's strongest instrument won in the register of sovereignty and the law of the sea, which belongs to no part of this field. A framework that scores everything as substitution or not will miss that third case, which is the one that passed.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable and privately owned, with no instrument settling who pays. Extended this week from hazard to sabotage and from Nepal to the North Sea: Dutch wind farms, cables and pipelines are the assets the state is trying to protect, their operators hold the data the state's own audit says is not being pooled, and the protection programme is funded at a sixth of what its minister asked for. The ownership problem is the same problem whether the threat is a flood or a shadow fleet, and it is that nobody can compel the private holder of a public dependency to share or to spend.

The climate referent and the security register are being decoupled, in both directions, by different actors in the same week. Out: NATO's resilience baseline keeps the weather and drops the word; a US presidential address drops both; India's foreign minister securitises finance, supply chains and technology and files climate under development. In: a British foreign secretary asks for climate in threat assessments; the Union's security chief co-hosts a ministers' dialogue on climate as a national security risk; an Australian prime minister opens Climate Week on climate security as national security. The two movements are not opposites and do not cancel. What they show is that the pairing of the referent with the register has become a discretionary rhetorical choice rather than an analytical commitment, which means counting mentions measures fashion. The thing to count instead is whether an instrument has a variable in it that changes when the climate changes.

open_threads.text: PSI's current funding phase. Advanced on the personnel discrepancy and not on the money. The institute's own pages refused retrieval for a third consecutive week, so the standing instruction to try another route was followed: the platform's separate team page opened and settles the job-title question that has been carried for three weeks. It lists Louise van Schaik as Senior Research Fellow and PSI Coordinator, Hannah Lentschig as PSI Project Leader, and Gen. Tom Middendorp (ret.) as Senior Research Associate and chairman of the military council — which also resolves, from the platform's own page, the association this digest has twice declined to state. The page carries no funding information and no phase date, so the funding half is unchanged: the only publicly datable phase announcement remains December 2019.

Whether NATO published a 4th Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, and the thread now has a much better answer than silence. NATO published the first substantial revision of its seven baseline requirements for resilience since 2016 on 15 September, releasing them publicly for the first time, with extreme weather, natural disasters and changing environmental conditions among the cross-cutting risks and the phrase climate change absent from the document (D4). The assessment series remains listed for 2022, 2023 and 2024 with nothing since. So the question was never going to be answered by another assessment: the work moved into a binding requirements text that cannot name its driver. Two readings of the page disagree about the date of its most recent item and both agree there is no 2025 or 2026 edition. The thread stays open only on whether NATO ever states what happened to the series.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Re-checked for a fourth consecutive week against the council's own site: no report since the 2024 edition and the most recent item of any kind still the open letter of 23 October 2025. One addition to the record, which resolves an unverified entry on the standing roster: the site lists Sherri Goodman, former US Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Environmental Security, as the council's Secretary General, alongside Gen. Tom Middendorp (ret.) as chair. A council with a chair, a secretary general and eleven months of silence is a body being kept in existence rather than run.

Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit. Advanced for the first time. Britain announced £1 million for it on 25 September inside a £331 million package, and its own programme pages confirm an extended third phase running 2026 to 2028, ten advisers deployed, the most recent onboarded to the Pacific Islands Forum in June, and fourteen contributing governments as of January. The unit is not being wound down. The trajectory is still not established: the trust fund that finances it lists a consolidated financial report for 2025 whose figures did not render from here, so annual volumes — the part that would show a direction rather than a data point — remain unread. The route is now known and the thread should close next time that report is opened.

Whether the 2028-2034 budget carries a security-tagged climate line. Not advanced, and the alternative route tried this week produced something better next door. The Parliament's research service briefing on the coming resilience framework, which did open, carries no budget-framework reference at all, but it does establish that climate resilience strategic plans are to be a precondition of access to Union funding and that adaptation investment needs are about €69 billion a year by 2050. Conditionality on access is a stronger instrument than an earmark and it is now the thing to look for; the earmark question stands unanswered.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate — gap, sixth week. The negative observable has hardened from an absence into a broken commitment. China's own foreign ministry text of the 25 August boundary talks commits both sides to holding the next China-India expert-level mechanism meeting on trans-border rivers in September, with hydrological data sharing and memorandum renewal on the agenda. September ended with no announcement that it happened. Meanwhile China continues supplying Nepal with daily basin data under no instrument, and a Nepali hydrologist reports that Chinese participants in May said they lacked authority to sign.

Any Indian security document on climate — gap, unchanged. India's general-debate statement of 26 September was built on a weaponisation of everything and named chokepoints in finance, markets, supply chains and technology, with climate handled separately and in the development-partnership register. The interesting qualification is that India's own climate-adjacent security demand is real and documented — upstream hydrological data and the technical details of the Yarlung Tsangpo cascade, pressed at the 6 August boundary-affairs meeting — and is pursued entirely through boundary diplomacy. There may never be a doctrinal text because the file is not filed under climate.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. The question is now judged to have been mis-framed and the reasons are in the pushback. The fund has disbursed nothing to anyone; at least 119 countries have requested about $2.8 billion; a June board meeting approved none of four requests; the next is in December. Nepal's claim is $20 million because that is the ceiling for a single project, against reconstruction needs of about $4.7 billion. An evidence standard is not the binding constraint on an instrument that has not made a decision. The thread stays open in a narrower form: what standard, if any, appears in the reasoning of the fund's first approval, whenever that comes.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment, and whether the review's concession that some damage will not be prevented is adopted or dropped. Second checkpoint passed with no answer at all. The cabinet's formal response to the 2027 programme, which in 2025 arrived one day after the programme was laid, could not be found twelve days after this year's. That absence is weaker than a verified one because the central government document register was reorganised earlier this year and could not be searched from here; it should be re-tested next week before any weight is put on it.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will now receive it. Unchanged on its own terms and demoted in priority. No fund board, development bank or court reasoned from adaptation limits this week, and the reason is now clearer: the fund that would be the first candidate has not adjudicated anything at all. The thread survives because the underlying observation survives — the vocabulary exists and the procedure does not, and the first body to reach for one sets the standard by default — but it should no longer be treated as the live constraint on the Nepal file.

Who bears roughly Rs300 billion of privately held losses in Nepal, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. Sharpened arithmetically and otherwise unmoved. The maximum single-project claim on the fund is $20 million; the assessed recovery bill is about $4.7 billion, of which about seventy per cent falls on private balance sheets. So the instrument cannot reach even the public share, which makes the question of whether it could reach the private share moot for now. Nothing appeared this week on insurance, on state recovery on behalf of private owners, or on the eight of thirteen privately held hydropower projects.

Whether any security institution reads the sea-level declaration as a security instrument. The declaration settles, as a matter of stated state practice, that statehood and maritime entitlements survive physical loss of territory — which is a first-order question about sovereignty, exclusive economic zones, fisheries and seabed resources, and nothing in the reachable record connects it to a defence ministry, an alliance staff, an intelligence body or a naval planner. Two things would confirm uptake: a security document citing the declaration, and a maritime-boundary or fisheries dispute in which a party invokes it. What would refute the thread is the more likely outcome: the instrument stays in the law-of-the-sea community and the security community never notices it.

Whether NATO's removal of the climate referent from its resilience baseline is a one-off drafting choice or the alliance's new standing practice. The 2026 requirements name extreme weather, natural disasters and changing environmental conditions and never say climate change; the announcement names neither. The American defence department adopted the same formula by memorandum in March 2025. What would confirm a standing practice: the next alliance strategy, ministerial communiqué or summit declaration using the hazard vocabulary without the referent. What would refute it: any alliance text naming climate change, or a revision of these requirements inside a few years rather than a decade. The second is the measurement that matters, because a requirement with no named driver cannot be revised as the driver changes.

Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains. Every other condition for anticipatory action is satisfied: a seasonal forecast at a hundred per cent probability of El Niño with a positive dipole, 23 of 26 models projecting a very strong event, named basins, specified measures published in June, and an exposure estimate of 2.5 to 3.5 million people with about a million likely to be displaced. The humanitarian plan asks $852 million for 2.4 million people and was set 40 per cent below last year's. This is the cleanest available test of whether the field's early-warning argument has any purchase on financing, and it has a deadline rather than an indicator.

Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Nothing from either capital by the close of the week. The proposal is designed so that silence is costly: it asks for the formalisation of data China is already supplying to Nepal daily, and it names the two states that failed to hold their own scheduled river-data meeting in the same month. A response of any kind, including a refusal, would be the first on-the-record Chinese or Indian position on a climate-security institution.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Unchanged and now worth a note about where food security actually went this month: into NATO's fourth baseline requirement, which obliges allies to hold exercised contingency plans for food and water supply in crisis and conflict (D4), and into the foreign ministers' statement of 24 September, which names fertilisers, food and water security (D1). The Council is not where the food-security file is being advanced.

The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Advanced on register rather than on money. Its only climate publication between 20 and 28 September was an analysis of NATO's new resilience requirements, by Erin Sikorsky and Noah Fritzhand on 21 September, and no new state briefer appeared. The international and doctrinal work is alive. Funding remains undocumented, and its own pages still name Sikorsky as director of both the institute and the military council, with Tom Ellison deputy and John Conger director emeritus.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next UNISFA mandate renewal. Unchanged. SIPRI's climate-security publication list still ends at the August study and shows nothing for September; a Lake Chad fact sheet listed earlier has still not been read. Open on the renewal.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The European integrated framework for climate resilience. Substantially advanced, and it is now the most consequential pending instrument in this digest. The Commission is scheduled to present it on 20 October, with a provisional Environment Council policy debate on 11 December. The package is a communication, a regulation, a recommendation and a Commission decision, and its legislative core includes a common European climate reference scenario based on a 3°C trajectory by 2100, resilience strategic plans as a condition of access to Union funding, and a duty to assign named risk owners for major climate risks. The standing date correction still holds: the call for evidence closed 4 September 2025.

Succession to the Secretary-General, finalisation expected in the autumn. A third straw poll was held on 18 September, three days before this window opened: Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica led with nine encourage votes to five discourage, with Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana on eight, and no candidate emerged who could clearly survive a veto. Eight candidates remain. A fourth poll was expected after high-level week and had not been scheduled by the close of this window; the Council aims to recommend a single name in October and the incumbent's term ends 31 December. Still nothing found on what any candidate has said about Council competence over climate, which remains the highest-value unanswered question here — and it is now urgent rather than interesting, because the Swiss presidency in October has named climate security a priority and the two files will be in the same room.

The November conference of the parties at Antalya, under a Türkiye-Australia presidency. Advanced on framing. The Australian co-host opened Climate Week in New York on 21 September on the theme that climate security is national security (D5), which is a presidency choosing the security frame over the ambition frame before the conference opens, and drew an immediate challenge from a former Australian chief of defence asking where the plan is given continuing coal and gas expansion. Nothing new found on the Turkish half, and the standing roster still has no named Turkish contact, which is now six weeks from the conference.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Decisively advanced on the second half and not at all on the first. The Secretary-General's summit of 23 September ran a dialogue titled Financing Adaptation in the Era of Overshoot and named adaptation in an era of overshoot as one of three priorities; the coming European resilience framework writes a 3°C reference scenario into draft law. No security institution used the term — and the one that legislated this month removed even the phrase climate change from its text. The gap between the civilian planning premise and the security vocabulary is now the finding.

Whether the small island states' legal-character defence of 1.5°C holds through the General Assembly session and the November conference. The alliance's own pages refused retrieval, so this rests on the record of the 24 September meeting, where Palau's president Surangel Whipps Jr. spoke for the alliance and said the climate crisis is not of their making, and on the declaration itself. The important observation is a redirection rather than a retreat: the legal-character argument won this week, and it won on statehood and maritime zones rather than on 1.5°C. A bloc whose leverage rests on legal character has just demonstrated that the character it can actually defend is sovereign, not thermal.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. Advanced in the only direction available: Nepal has proposed the institution (D3), naming glacial-lake monitoring and joint early warning as functions of a trilateral mechanism with India and China. No funding, no response from either named state, and no data-sharing agreement. The attribution study's conclusion that no existing system could have given sufficient lead time still cuts against warning as the missing piece for this specific hazard, which makes the proposal's emphasis on glacial lakes worth watching: lake monitoring is not what failed in August.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Superseded in practice. Nepal's posture is now unambiguously outward and institutional rather than defensive: a prime ministerial proposal for a trilateral mechanism, a public description of the existing financing instruments as grossly inadequate, and a continuing reconstruction-finance circuit through lenders. The inward-facing question about assistance limits has not recurred and should be closed next week unless something revives it.

Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Second checkpoint passed with silence rather than an answer: no cabinet response to the 2027 programme found twelve days after it was laid, against one day in 2025, with the caveat about the reorganised document register recorded in section C. The autumn estimates debates are the next opportunity.

Whether Nepal's reconstruction bill produces a loss and damage response, and on what evidentiary basis. The arithmetic is now the answer and it is not an evidentiary one. The claim is at the instrument's per-project ceiling of $20 million against about $4.7 billion of assessed need; the fund has disbursed nothing to anyone; at least 119 countries are queued for about $2.8 billion; the next board meeting is in December. Note the separate and easily confused fact, which some reporting this week got wrong: the $20 million confirmed to Nepal in early September is for proposals predating the disaster and is awaiting a reviewer's comments before release.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether NATO ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement, and the question has been overtaken by a better one. The alliance published a revised and, for the first time, public set of resilience baseline requirements on 15 September with the hazard retained and the referent removed (D4). The analytical work did not stop; it changed vehicles and lost its name. This move should now be tracked as the removal of the referent rather than as the lapse of a report.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. No movement in either direction: no fund board, bank or court reasoned from adaptation limits, and no security institution used the argument that a hazard class has outrun early warning. One thing that would have counted as refutation has not happened either — the finding is not yet being widely miscited as an event attribution. The attribution network published nothing new this week, which under the corrected rule is evidence about nothing.

Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern. First real counter-evidence: no new state briefer appeared, and the institute's only climate item in the window was international and doctrinal (D4 analysis, 21 September). The second measurement, a second institute writing climate security for statehouses, has not fired. The nearest thing is a Berlin convening on 22 September of German and American experts on how state governments, regional electricity markets and utilities shape American energy policy — a sub-federal turn in transatlantic energy engagement with no security content, which is adjacent and does not count.

Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates, or is corrected by amendment. No response found and no amendment. What the parliamentary week did contain is the other half of the same argument: a committee session on protecting North Sea infrastructure, a file where the responsible minister asked for €70 million a year and received €12.1 million in bridge funding, and where the Court of Audit found in May that an information hub adopted by cabinet has stalled over who pays. The general form of the question is unchanged and is getting a consistent answer: this government funds what can be built or procured and not what has to be coordinated.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Commitments to horizon scanning inside national and regional security systems, to joint risk assessments and scenario and contingency planning, to work on fertilisers, food and water security, early warning and anticipatory action, the development banks' crisis toolkits, and the embedding of climate security in United Nations agencies. No secretariat, no next meeting, no deliverable and no money. The joint risk assessment is the testable commitment because it produces a document; the named milestones are the November conference, the Bank and Fund annual meetings and continuing engagement through 2027.

Britain's £331 million for climate-driven instability, of which £330 million goes to the Global Environment Facility and £1 million to the joint United Nations climate security unit. Open on whether the proportion is a one-off or the going rate: the test is whether the next British climate-security announcement moves money into instruments that do climate security rather than environment, and whether the £1 million recurs or was a gesture for a week when the vocabulary was in fashion.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China, to share satellite data, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, run joint early warning and coordinate cross-border assistance. Open on whether either named state responds, and on whether the mechanism acquires a convenor, a date or a funder. A refusal would be as informative as agreement and neither has come.

NATO's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September: extreme weather, natural disasters and changing environmental conditions among the cross-cutting risks, an all-hazards food and water contingency requirement, an energy requirement covering cascading impacts, and the phrase climate change nowhere in the document. Open on whether allies report against the new food and water requirement, on whether the referent stays out of subsequent alliance texts, and on how long until the next revision — the last interval was ten years and a text with no named driver has nothing to revise against.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, by a co-president of the November conference, and the immediate challenge to it from a former Australian chief of defence asking where the plan is. Open on whether a plan appears before Antalya, and on whether the presidency carries the security frame into the conference's own agenda or drops it once the negotiation starts.
